notes:
I worked through 27 verses using a limited number of searches and page reads. Enduring Word (David Guzik) loaded only up to vv. 14–17. I got its notes on the Sabbath section (vv. 19–27) from search results instead. I didn't open any netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, oca.org or catholic.com page, and I found nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter, so those are left out. Verses with no sourced notes are skipped.

---

## Part 1: The traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1**
- Guzik: the iron pen and diamond point show how hard and deep Judah's rebellion was. There was nothing superficial about their sinful state. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-17/
- Guzik also says both the heart and the people's religious practice were marked by sin. He quotes Feinberg that the "altars" may be to the altars of Baal. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-17/
- Pulpit Commentary: "Judah's sin" here means their idolatry in practice, not just a tendency to sin. The altar horns may be in view because they were smeared with sacrificial blood. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/17.htm
- Matthew Henry: The sin of sinners is never forgotten till it is forgiven. Their own consciences act as witnesses against them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_017.cfm
- Bible Hub's study page says the Hebrew word for "engraved" (charut) stresses how permanent and deep the sin is. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/jeremiah/17.htm

**v. 2**
- Guzik: like an inscription on stone, the sin would set a course for later generations. Their sin was written so deep and in such places that it would be read for generations. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-17/
- Pulpit admits the link to v. 1 is unclear. It reads the verse as showing that the people's thoughts turn to idol altars whenever they pass a leafy tree or high hill. It rejects the Hitzig/Keil reading ("as they remember their children…") as unnatural. It also says "groves" should be Asherah idols. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/17.htm

**v. 3**
- Pulpit calls this verse even harder to read. It argues "my mountain in the field" is Mount Zion, the site of the temple, rather than Jerusalem being addressed. It notes that Ewald thinks the text may be corrupted, following the wording of 15:13. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/17.htm
- Bible Hub's study page: "high places" (bamot) were raised sites used for idol worship. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/jeremiah/17.htm

**v. 4**
- Matthew Henry hears an echo of the law that the land must rest one year in seven. Because they ignored it, God would now force the land to rest. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_017.cfm
- Pulpit agrees the word alludes to Exodus 23:11 and Deuteronomy 15:2. It thinks the text is "rather out of order" and offers "thou shalt let loose thy hand" as a fix. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/17.htm
- Constable quotes a writer who sees irony here: Judah has forsaken or abandoned her covenantal inheritance. So God hands Judah over to exile. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-17.html
- Henry on "burn forever": the anger burns so fiercely it seems endless, and it will be so unless they repent. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_017.cfm

**v. 5**
- Guzik: the curse follows naturally from trusting weak human beings. You cannot make flesh your strength without your heart also turning from the LORD. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-17/
- Pulpit: "God and man, flesh and spirit" are natural opposites, as in Isaiah 31:3. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/17.htm
- Bible Hub's study notes link the verse to Judah repeatedly turning to foreign nations instead of the Lord. https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/17-5.htm
- GotQuestions gives it an eternal edge: those who trust in man are cursed and destined to miss eternity in heaven. https://www.gotquestions.org/trusts-in-man-cursed.html

**v. 6**
- Guzik pictures a dry desert shrub close to death. He cites Tverberg: the plant may be the Arar, whose name sounds like the Hebrew for "cursed" (arur). It bears hollow, dusty fruit (the "Sodom apple") and looks healthy while being empty. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-17/
- Pulpit: Jerome thought of a tamarisk, Tristram of the dwarf juniper. Most scholars take the word as an adjective meaning "destitute." "Shall not see" means will not feel or experience. A "salt land" means completely barren ground. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/17.htm

**vv. 7–8**
- Guzik: Jeremiah is drawing on Psalm 1. He quotes Thompson that Psalm 1 may have been available to the prophet. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-17/
- Pulpit: in v. 8 the Hebrew text reads "shall not fear," supported by the Septuagint, Peshitta and Vulgate. The KJV's "shall not see" comes from a margin reading. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/17.htm
- Benson: trusting the Lord rightly means walking closely with him and not drifting from him in heart. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/17-7.htm
- Gill reads the trust as trust in Christ, the Word of God. He draws on the Targum's "the Word of the Lord." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/17-7.htm
- Constable reads vv. 7–8 partly as Jeremiah's own testimony that he has come through a dry period. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-17.html

**v. 9**
- Ellicott links it to what comes before: if blessing and curse are so plain, why do people choose the curse? Because of self-deceit that blinds them. He prefers the translation "incurably diseased." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/17-9.htm
- Barnes likewise renders it "mortally sick." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/17-9.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: "deceitful" comes from the root behind Jacob's name ("supplanter"). Judah followed Jacob's deceit but not his faith. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/17-9.htm
- Pulpit: Delitzsch reads it as "proud" (literally uneven or rugged). The Septuagint renders it "deep." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/17.htm
- Gill: the verse speaks first to Judah but is true of every human heart. He says it is more deceitful to a person than the devil, because it is nearer. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/17-9.htm
- Guzik applies it against the advice to "follow your heart." Quoting Harrison, he says the Hebrew points more to sickness than to depravity. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-17/
- GotQuestions connects the verse to total depravity. It explains this does not mean everyone is as bad as possible, but that no one can turn themselves around. https://www.gotquestions.org/heart-desperately-wicked.html

**v. 10**
- Guzik: God searches what we cannot know about ourselves, so it is wise to trust his verdict over our feelings. He quotes Thompson that "heart and kidneys" cover all the hidden parts of a person. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-17/
- Benson pictures God testing the heart the way gold is tested, or a prisoner is tried, before judging. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/17-9.htm
- Bible Hub's study page links this verse to Revelation 2:23, where Christ uses the same words of himself. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/jeremiah/17.htm

**v. 11**
- Guzik: this proverb warns against trusting riches. Only riches gained wrongly are condemned. He cites the folk belief that the partridge hatched other birds' eggs. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-17/
- Pulpit: the prophet takes a popular belief and uses it. Canon Tristram rejected the belief as bad natural history, but Pulpit says the grammar still requires this sense. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/17.htm
- Matthew Henry: the wealth stays behind at death, but the guilt goes with the person. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_017.cfm

**v. 12**
- Guzik: God, enthroned at the temple, is the contrast to every false trust. He quotes G. Campbell Morgan calling this one of the greatest words of the Old Testament. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-17/
- Pulpit translates it as words addressed to God: "Thou throne of glory… thou hope of Israel." It explains that the temple was the place of God's Name. Adding v. 13 keeps it from sounding like the empty temple slogan of 7:4. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/17.htm
- Lange: Zion, chosen from eternity, is in concept God's eternal dwelling. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lcc/jeremiah-17.html

**v. 13**
- Pulpit: "written in the earth" contrasts with the iron-pen record of v. 1. The sudden "from me" is awkward, and the Vulgate reads "from thee." "Fountain of living waters" is a favourite phrase of Jeremiah's (2:13). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/17.htm
- Bible Hub's study notes: Jesus takes the "living water" image for himself in John 4 and 7. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/jeremiah/17.htm

**v. 14**
- Guzik: whether the healing is physical or spiritual "doesn't really matter," because God meets both needs. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-17/
- Pulpit: Jeremiah is one of the "broken in heart" whom only God can heal (Psalm 147:3). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/17.htm

**v. 15**
- Pulpit: the mockers treat Jeremiah as a false prophet under Deuteronomy 18:22, since his warnings had not yet come true. Keil therefore dates this before the first Babylonian invasion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/17.htm
- Matthew Henry: they mocked God's patience and used it to question whether he tells the truth. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_017.cfm

**v. 16**
- Guzik: Jeremiah preached judgment but did not want it to come. It was painful for him to deliver. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-17/
- Henry: ministers, like God, must not wish for sinners' death. Though we warn of the woeful day, we must not wish for it, but rather weep because of it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_017.cfm
- Pulpit: Jeremiah is an "under-shepherd" waiting on God's will. The word for "woeful" is the same one used for "desperately wicked" in v. 9. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/17.htm

**v. 17**
- Pulpit: Jeremiah asks that God not shame him by leaving his prophecies unfulfilled. "A consternation" would be a better translation than "a terror." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/17.htm
- Lange quotes Zinzendorf: it is hard when your refuge becomes a terror, but discipline ends in glory. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lcc/jeremiah-17.html

**v. 18**
- Pulpit calls this a "terrible execration" (a curse). It takes "double" to mean "amply sufficient." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/17.htm
- Henry softens it: let the persecutors be overcome by the conviction of God's word, or else let the threatened judgment come. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_017.cfm
- Constable notes that Jeremiah's suffering seemed to contradict v. 7's promise that trust brings blessing. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-17.html

**vv. 19–20**
- Guzik on the gate: quoting a source, he says it is "of uncertain location" and was used by people other than priests and Levites. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-17/
- Barnes thinks it may be the main temple entrance, where there was probably trade in sacrifices. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/17-21.html
- Coffman: no particular gate is meant. Jeremiah preached wherever the people were. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/17-21.html
- Henry: the message went first to the court gate, because rulers are responsible for keeping the Sabbath. He dates it to Josiah's reform. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_017.cfm

**vv. 21–22**
- Barnes: country people came for temple worship but brought produce to trade. Both sides avoided manual labour but did not think buying and selling broke the commandment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/17-21.htm
- Keil: the burdens point mainly to market trade. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/17-21.htm
- Calvin: carrying burdens through Jerusalem's gates was like openly scorning God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/17-21.html
- Henry and Poole read "take heed to your souls" as meaning the inner attitude matters for keeping the Sabbath. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/jeremiah/17.htm

**v. 23**
- Guzik: kings and commoners alike rejected the word and treated the Sabbath like any other day. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-17/

**vv. 24–26**
- Guzik calls the Sabbath a "test case" for whether they had truly repented. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-17/
- Pulpit: "shall remain forever" should read "shall be inhabited forever." It asks whether "and princes" slipped in by accident, comparing 22:4. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/17.htm
- Henry: Whatever supports religion tends to establish the civil interests of a land. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_017.cfm

**v. 27**
- Ellicott: the fire is figurative rather than literal. It stands for God's anger, though an actual fire may have been how it came. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/17-27.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: the punishment matches the sin, with burdens at the gates answered by fire in the gates. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/17-27.htm
- Henry: an enemy besieging the gates would light the fire. It was fulfilled when the Babylonians took the city (Jer. 52:13). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/jeremiah/17.htm

## Part 2: Where Protestant traditions differ

**v. 9: Is the Christian's heart still "deceitful and desperately wicked"?**
- *Baptist (John Piper, Desiring God):* the verse is true of every human heart. But where the new covenant applies there is a new creation: the Holy Spirit is given and a new nature is formed. https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/is-the-christians-heart-deceitfully-wicked
- *Calvary Chapel (Guzik):* the believer has a new heart and identity, so we are not deceitful at the core. Still, some inward deceit and wickedness remains to be dealt with. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-17/
- *Reformed Baptist (Gill):* only a spiritual person knows the plague of his heart, and even then not fully. Gill says "the Pharisee and perfectionist" do not know their hearts, or they would not claim to be without sin. This is an anti-perfectionist point. I found no Wesleyan reply to it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/17-9.htm
- *Methodist (Benson):* the fallen heart is deceitful above all things, but Benson stresses a second, practical reading. We can fool ourselves that we trust God when we don't, and this shows when our hopes rise and fall with how circumstances look. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/17-9.htm
- *Evangelical (GotQuestions):* uses the verse to support "total depravity" in its Reformed sense. https://www.gotquestions.org/heart-desperately-wicked.html

**v. 5: Free will and grace**
- *Reformed (Calvin's Institutes, on monergism.com):* Calvin cites this verse against the pleasant idea of having enough virtue of our own to rest in. https://www.monergism.com/thethreshold/articles/onsite/deprived.html
- *Puritan (Matthew Henry):* those who rely on their own righteousness and think they can do without Christ "make flesh their arm." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/17-9.htm

**vv. 21–27: Does the Sabbath command apply to Christians?**
- *Puritan/Presbyterian (Matthew Henry):* he preaches these verses as a sermon on keeping the Sabbath holy and applies them in detail. No loaded carts, porters or errands on that day. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_017.cfm He also writes that the streams of all religion run either deep or shallow according as the banks of the sabbath are kept up or neglected. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_017.cfm
- *Calvin:* cites v. 24 to show how seriously God treats the Sabbath. Few commands are repeated more often. https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/comment3/comm_vol04/htm/v.htm
- *Geneva Bible notes:* breaking this one command makes them breakers of the whole law. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/17-21.htm
- *Other evangelical readers keep it within the old covenant:* Constable says God commanded the Sabbath "as the Mosaic Covenant specified." Coffman sees the command standing for the whole Mosaic Law. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/17-21.html Guzik treats it as a test of Judah's repentance and does not say it binds Christians. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-17/
- I found no Lutheran, Pentecostal or Anglican source that discusses this chapter directly.

## Part 3: Other views

**Modern and critical scholarship (from the older critical commentaries; I couldn't reach the NET Bible notes)**
- vv. 19–27: Pulpit records that Geiger and Rowland Williams thought the Sabbath section was added later to support the reforms of Ezra and Nehemiah. Pulpit notes that it doesn't connect with what surrounds it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/17.htm
- vv. 9–13: the Cambridge Bible calls this three separate pieces in different metres. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/17-9.htm It also reports Duhm's view that vv. 9–10 belong with v. 14. On that view, Jeremiah is confessing his own sin and God replies. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/17-9.htm
- vv. 3–4: Pulpit flags likely damage to the text in both verses. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/17.htm

**Catholic and Orthodox**
- v. 5: Augustine used this verse against the Pelagians, who held that people can choose good without grace. He argues "flesh" means human frailty and "arm" means power in action. The curse falls on anyone who hopes in himself for righteous living. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1510.htm
- v. 5: In a letter, Augustine warns Palatinus not to trust in his own strength, because cursed is everyone who trusts in man. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1102218.htm
- v. 5: Against the Donatists, he uses the verse to say no one should boast in a human leader. https://ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf104.v.v.v.ii.html
- v. 9: the Catholic Douay-Rheims reads "perverse… and unsearchable," following the Vulgate. https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/17-9.htm
